output.diagnosis: A 40% increase in email signups is not sufficient evidence to keep the discount popup. The popup may create incremental customer value through email capture, but it may also suppress immediate conversion, reduce AOV, or reduce gross profit through the discount. The decision should be based on incremental gross profit per visitor over the full customer journey, not opt-in rate alone.

actions.action: Run a randomized holdout test: expose most eligible visitors to the popup and withhold it from a smaller control group. A 90% exposed / 10% holdout split is a practical example, not a required allocation.

Persist the experiment assignment at visitor level and tag both groups in analytics, ecommerce, and email systems. Follow visitors from first session through purchase and subsequent email-attributed purchases.

Set gross profit per visitor as the decision metric if product, discount, shipping/fulfilment, and payment-cost data are available. Calculate revenue net of the popup discount and subtract relevant variable costs. If that is not currently feasible, use revenue per visitor as an interim outcome and explicitly treat margin as unresolved.

Measure supporting outcomes by test group: purchase conversion rate, revenue per visitor, AOV, gross margin or gross profit per order, discount redemption, email opt-in rate, unsubscribe rate, repeat purchase revenue, refund/return rate, and email-driven revenue.

Use guardrails to identify harm that opt-in growth can hide: immediate conversion rate, AOV, gross profit per visitor, site performance, refund rate, and unsubscribe rate. A higher signup rate should not override deterioration in these commercial outcomes.

Predefine the keep/modify/remove rule before reading results. Keep the popup only if the exposed group shows a credible positive net commercial result without unacceptable guardrail deterioration. Remove or redesign it if signup gains are offset by lower conversion, lower order value, or discount-driven margin loss.

If the current popup is not profitable, test alternatives rather than assuming popups should be removed: later trigger timing, exit-intent display, fewer impressions, a non-discount value proposition, a smaller or different incentive, or targeting only new visitors. Test one major change at a time against an appropriate control.

For analysis, recognize that revenue and profit per visitor are noisy because most visitors spend nothing and a small number place large orders. Consider capping/winsorizing extreme order values or reporting a threshold purchase metric alongside the primary metric. If your testing platform supports CUPED and you have stable pre-experiment user identifiers, enable it; it may offer limited benefit for mostly new anonymous visitors.

missing_information: Popup eligibility and trigger rules: entry, time delay, scroll depth, exit intent, frequency cap, device, geography, traffic source, and whether existing subscribers are excluded.
The exact discount: amount or percentage, minimum spend, product exclusions, stackability, expiry, and redemption rate.
Baseline and post-popup conversion rate, AOV, revenue per visitor, and their changes by traffic source and device.
Product-level gross margins and variable costs, including the cost of the discount, shipping subsidy, fulfilment, payment fees, free gifts, and expected refunds/returns.
Whether the popup captures email only or SMS as well, and the downstream email program: welcome sequence, deliverability, unsubscribe rate, and purchase attribution window.
Visitor identity and tracking capability across sessions and email clicks, including consent requirements and how test assignment will be retained.
Traffic volume, expected test duration, and the business-relevant minimum effect needed to make a decision.
Whether the popup affects repeat purchase behavior, customer support burden, brand perception, or discount dependence.
caveats: Do not infer incremental revenue or profitability from the reported 40% signup lift.
The 90/10 holdout split is an example from the supplied guidance; the appropriate allocation and duration depend on traffic, outcome variability, and risk tolerance.
Gross profit per visitor is the most decision-relevant metric here, but it is noisier than conversion rate and requires accurate cost data.
Email-attributed revenue alone can overstate value if it ignores purchases that would have happened without the popup or if attribution rules differ between groups.
Avoid ending the test based only on an early opt-in result; evaluate the prespecified full-funnel outcomes after sufficient follow-up for the discount and email sequence to operate.

input.task: Our popup increased email signups. How do we decide whether to keep it?
input.brand: DTC coffee brand; email signups rose 40% after adding a discount popup; revenue impact and margin impact are unknown.
input.knowledge:
[6669a87c07bb0d8b50b848a5] Test popups and features with a holdout to capture net revenue
Use when: A team believes a popup (or another on-site feature) helps or hurts and wants evidence beyond opt-in rate.
- Split traffic so one group sees the feature and a smaller holdout does not — the source's popup example uses 90% exposed and 10% holdout.
- Tag and track both groups through the full customer journey rather than stopping at opt-in.
- Measure revenue per visitor, AOV, conversion rate and email/SMS opt-in rates so you can see whether opt-in gains are offset by conversion suppression.
- Apply the same pattern to features: hold back about 5% of users from product recommendations and compare incremental revenue.
- Conclude on net incremental revenue — the source stresses that opt-in lift alone does not establish value.
Caveat: The source gives the 90/10 and 5% splits as examples without required sample sizes or durations.
Caveat: The source does not report popup results, so no expected effect size is implied.

[aa58bde3f9d7ce21f106f0c8] Use a positioned bundle and threshold to raise revenue per visitor
Use when: Designing the offer on a landing page or cart for a product that already works as a single.
- Build a routine bundle rather than a single item; the source's example moves from a single overnight repair serum to a bundle of cleanser, serum and night cream.
- Bake a discount across the bundle rather than discounting the product outright: the source argues the discount costs no margin because it only passes on the shipping and fulfilment economies of scale from sending three items together.
- Use the free gift to improve the break-even return on ad spend rather than cutting price; the source's example gives away a $14 item with minimal margin impact and a $4 gift.
- Use a free-shipping threshold and an upsell together, since both increase revenue per visitor; a threshold also objection-handles the top abandonment reason.
- Add a one-click post-purchase upsell: bill the card already on file without re-entering details, presented right after checkout when the buyer is warmest.
- In the cart slide-out, upsell a routine or bundle to unlock the free gifts and shipping rather than showing only the single item.
Caveat: The $122 bundle and its components come from an illustrative landing page, not a store result.
Caveat: Bundling depends on your own shipping and fulfilment costs; no calculation method is given.
Caveat: Post-purchase upsell take rate is described only as very high with no figures.

[a2f6516fce1f6a9a7d85a1b2] Use threshold and post-purchase upsells instead of discounting everything
Use when: Deciding how to raise AOV when the single product already converts.
- Avoid across-the-board discounting, which the source says trains customers to wait for discounts.
- Use a free-shipping or free-gift threshold to lift order value instead of cutting price.
- Add a post-purchase one-click upsell tied to what the customer just bought, since they are warmest immediately after spending.
- Keep the main landing page offer positioned around solving the customer's problem in three steps rather than around price, so margin is preserved.
- If you want to test shipping thresholds or gift levels, do it as a genuine test with enough volume, not as a permanent blanket cut.
Caveat: The source gives no take-rate figures for post-purchase upsells, only that they are very high.
Caveat: Whether a limited time window is required to make the upsell work is not stated.

[438f0a28f54c6f4f5b7caf9e] CUPED variance reduction and its ceiling on DTC traffic
Use when: Evaluating whether to turn on CUPED in your testing platform, or looking for faster ways to reach power on a DTC store.
- Understand the method: CUPED (Controlled-experiment Using Pre-Experiment Data; Deng, Xu, Kohavi, Walker, Microsoft 2013) uses pre-experiment data — usually the same metric measured before the test — as a covariate to strip out variance not caused by the treatment. The adjusted estimator stays unbiased but has lower variance, so you reach significance faster or detect smaller effects at the same sample.
- Know the optimistic figure: Optimizely's glossary claims it can cut sample requirements 30-50% for metrics with strong correlation to historical behaviour. It is now default-on in several tools (Datadog, Optimizely) and used by Netflix, Airbnb and Booking.
- Check the DTC practicality: CUPED needs pre-experiment data keyed to the same user, which means logged-in users or stable device IDs. For a DTC brand where most checkout traffic is new or not logged in, the pre-period covariate is often missing or weakly correlated, so the variance reduction is smaller.
- See the ceiling evidence: Jin, Ba and colleagues at LinkedIn ran CUPED on n=400,000 feed members and found it reduces 15.91% of variance versus the difference-in-means estimator, limited because member revenue is volatile with weak autocorrelation across periods.
- Verdict: turn it on if your platform offers it and you have returning identified users; it is not a magic fix for a brand with mostly new, anonymous traffic.
- Use the simpler cousins that help ecommerce more: pick a proportion metric instead of a raw revenue mean, and winsorize (cap) outlier orders.
Caveat: Do not expect 30-50% sample reduction on mostly anonymous DTC traffic.
Caveat: CUPED does not remove the skew of order value; winsorization addresses that separately.

[638480d6003666b23f305fa2] Choosing a primary metric: conversion rate, RPV, or gross profit per visitor
Use when: Specifying the decision metric for a test, especially when someone proposes revenue per visitor on a modest-traffic store.
- Know conversion rate's profile: binary, low variance, fastest to power. Blind spot: it ignores order value.
- Know revenue per visitor (RPV): it captures conversion and AOV together, but revenue is highly skewed — in a typical ecommerce case 97% of visitors spend $0 and a few spend a lot, so the coefficient of variation can be around 750% (sd $18 on a mean of $2.40). This needs roughly 6x the traffic of a conversion-rate test for the same relative MDE — about 175,000 vs 28,000 per variant at a 3% baseline.
- Know gross profit per visitor: the honest objective for a DTC brand because it prices in margin and discounting, but it carries the same variance problem as RPV plus the need for margin data.
- Mitigate the variance rather than abandoning the metric: winsorize (cap) outlier orders or use a threshold proportion metric (share of visitors who spend more than $X) so no single large order dominates.
- Pair the primary with guardrails: AOV, return rate, refund rate, page load, add-to-cart and margin. A conversion win that tanks AOV or margin is not a win.
- Note the ecommerce pattern where higher conversion rate can yield lower revenue — attribute that example to the source, not to your own test before running it.
Caveat: The source does not specify the exact winsorizing threshold or the $X for a threshold proportion metric.
Caveat: RPV availability differs by platform; verify your tool's metric definitions.
